## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Asilakkhaṇajātaka* (Ja 126), translated as *Lucky Swords*, is a story preserved in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the narrative framework set at Jetavana, the Buddha related the tale concerning a sword-divining brahmin (*asilakkhaṇapāṭhaka*) retained by the King of Kosala to inspect newly forged swords and evaluate whether they were auspicious [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. The corrupt brahmin praised only the craftsmanship of smiths who offered him bribes and disparaged the rest [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. The thematic verse encapsulates the unpredictability of fortunes—how the very same circumstance can lead to benefit for one person yet ruin for another: through a sneeze, a prince wins a kingdom and a bride, whereas a sneezing brahmin loses his nose [Anandajoti 2010]. At the conclusion of the discourse, the Buddha identifies the nephew king as the Bodhisatta and the sword diviner as the Kosalan brahmin of the present [Fausböll 1877].
